entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: No longer used or useful because something newer or better has replaced it.
entries.usage: Common for technology, equipment, skills, jobs and rules: *obsolete equipment*, *an obsolete law*. The patterns *become obsolete* and *make* (formal: *render*) *something obsolete* are very frequent. For clothes, ideas or people that are just old-fashioned, *outdated* or *dated* is more natural; *obsolete* means nobody really uses it anymore.
entries.pattern: become obsolete; make / render something obsolete; obsolete equipment / technology / law
examples: Once everyone had GPS on their phones, the paper road maps in our glove box became **obsolete**.
Many truck drivers worry that self-driving vehicles will make their skills **obsolete** within twenty years.
The city finally repealed an **obsolete** law that banned bicycles on Main Street after dark.

drill.sentence: The new bridge made the old ferry service {{obsolete}}, and the last boat crossed the river in 2019.
drill.hint: no longer used because something better replaced it (not *unnecessary*, *redundant* or *outdated*)

entries.related: *outdated* — old-fashioned, but maybe still in use; *redundant* — not needed because something else does the same job; *cutting-edge* — the newest, the opposite.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: For a period of time with no fixed end, so nobody knows when it will stop.
entries.usage: Typical in official announcements and news: *postponed / suspended / closed indefinitely*, *on hold indefinitely*. It often suggests the pause may be long or even permanent. In conversation, *can't go on like this indefinitely* is a common way to say a situation must change.
entries.pattern: postpone / suspend / close / delay something indefinitely; can't go on indefinitely
examples: The concert has been postponed **indefinitely** because the lead singer injured her voice.
The bakery on our corner closed **indefinitely** after a kitchen fire, and nobody knows if it'll reopen.
You can't keep putting off the dentist **indefinitely**; that tooth will only get worse.

drill.sentence: Work on the new stadium has been put on hold {{indefinitely}}, and the city won't say when it might start again.
drill.hint: with no set end date (not *temporarily*)

entries.related: *temporarily* — for a limited time; *permanently* — forever; *for the foreseeable future* — for as long as anyone can predict now.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To describe or show someone or something in a particular way, for example in a film, book, painting or news report.
entries.usage: Very common for media and art, mostly in the pattern *portray someone as* + adjective or noun (*portrayed as a hero*). It is often used when the picture is selective or unfair (*The show portrays teachers as lazy*). Actors also *portray* characters, although *play* is the everyday verb; the noun is *portrayal*.
entries.pattern: portray someone / something as + adjective / noun; portray a character
examples: The documentary **portrays** the town as a quiet farming village, but it's really a busy commuter suburb.
He's best known for **portraying** a grumpy detective in a long-running TV series.
My brother always **portrays** himself as the victim when he tells the story of our road trip.

drill.sentence: In her memoir, the author {{portrays}} her father as a strict but loving man who rarely showed his feelings.
drill.hint: shows him in a certain way (not *describes*, *depicts*, *paints* or *presents*)

entries.related: *depict* — show in a picture or description, more neutral; *represent* — stand for or show; *portrayal* — the noun (*a sympathetic portrayal*).

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To say publicly that you support or approve of a person, product, plan or idea.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and marketing: athletes and celebrities *endorse* products (usually for money), and groups or newspapers *endorse* candidates or proposals. The noun *endorsement* is just as frequent (*a celebrity endorsement*). In the US you also *endorse a check* by signing the back of it, which is a separate sense.
entries.pattern: endorse + a product / a plan / a candidate / an idea; a celebrity endorsement
examples: The basketball star earns more from **endorsing** sneakers than from his actual salary.
The neighborhood association voted to **endorse** the plan for a new dog park.
I'm not **endorsing** this diet; I'm just saying it worked for my sister.

drill.sentence: Several famous chefs have {{endorsed}} the new cookware brand, and their faces are printed on every box.
drill.hint: publicly given their support to, often for money (not *promoted* or *backed*)

entries.related: *back* — support, more informal; *recommend* — tell someone something is good; *approve* — officially accept.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Logical and clear, with all the parts connected in a way that makes sense.
entries.usage: Used for plans, strategies, arguments and explanations: *a coherent plan*, *a coherent argument*. For a person, it means able to speak clearly and sensibly, often in the negative after an accident or a long night (*He was barely coherent*). The opposite *incoherent* is very common too (*an incoherent rant*).
entries.pattern: a coherent plan / strategy / argument / story; barely / not coherent
examples: The company has lots of good ideas but no **coherent** strategy for turning them into products.
After twenty hours of travel, I was too tired to give anyone a **coherent** answer.
The new bus routes finally form a **coherent** network instead of a tangle of lines that never meet.

drill.sentence: Her essay has some great ideas, but they jump around so much that the argument as a whole isn't {{coherent}}.
drill.hint: logically connected so that it holds together (not *clear*, *logical* or *consistent*)

entries.related: *consistent* — not contradicting itself; *cohesive* — united and working well together, of groups or texts; *incoherent* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Extreme and sudden, with a strong effect, often in a way that seems harsh.
entries.usage: Most common with *measures*, *action*, *changes*, *cuts* and *steps*: *take drastic action*. It often suggests a last resort, and *Isn't that a bit drastic?* is a typical reaction to an extreme plan. Unlike German *drastisch*, it does not mean vivid or explicit; for violent or crude images, English says *graphic*.
entries.pattern: drastic measures / action / changes / cuts; take drastic steps
examples: Quitting your job just because of one bad week seems a little **drastic**.
The school district made **drastic** cuts to its music program after the budget fell short.
His doctor warned him that without **drastic** changes to his diet, he'd need heart surgery.

drill.sentence: The water shortage got so bad that the town took {{drastic}} measures, like banning lawn watering and closing the public pool.
drill.hint: sudden and severe (not *extreme*, *strict*, *desperate* or *emergency*)

mistake.wrong: The movie shows the war in very drastic detail.
mistake.right: The movie shows the war in very graphic detail.
mistake.why: For violent or explicit images, English uses *graphic*; *drastic* is about extreme actions and changes, unlike German *drastisch*.

entries.related: *radical* — changing the basis of something; *extreme* — more general; *modest* — small, the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To consist of or be made up of particular parts or members.
entries.usage: Formal, common in reports, news and real estate or legal texts. The traditional pattern is that the whole *comprises* all its parts (*The team comprises five engineers*). *Is comprised of* is very common, but many editors still mark it as wrong, so in careful writing use *comprises*, *consists of* or *is made up of*.
entries.pattern: the whole comprises + the parts (= consists of / is made up of)
examples: The apartment **comprises** two bedrooms, a small kitchen and a balcony facing the park.
The school's advisory board **comprises** five parents, two teachers and the principal.
The festival program **comprises** more than forty concerts over three weekends.

drill.sentence: The museum's collection {{comprises}} about 3,000 paintings, most of them by local artists.
drill.hint: is made up of — formal, one word (not *includes* or *contains*)

mistake.wrong: The committee is comprised of nine members.
mistake.right: The committee comprises nine members. / The committee consists of nine members.
mistake.why: Many editors and style guides still treat *is comprised of* as an error, so formal writing avoids it.

entries.related: *consist of* — same meaning, neutral; *be made up of* — plainer; *include* — names only some of the parts, while *comprise* names all of them.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Based on observation, measurement or experiment rather than on theory or pure logic.
entries.usage: Common in science, economics and policy writing: *empirical evidence*, *empirical data*, *an empirical study*, *empirically tested*. In a discussion, *There's no empirical evidence for that* is a polite but firm way to reject a claim. The opposite is usually *theoretical*, and the weak kind of evidence is called *anecdotal*.
entries.pattern: empirical evidence / data / research / support; an empirical study / question
examples: There's no **empirical** evidence that cracking your knuckles causes arthritis.
Before changing the menu, the café owner took an **empirical** approach and tracked which dishes actually sold.
The theory predicts a strong effect, but we haven't tested it in the lab yet, so we have no **empirical** support.

drill.sentence: Plenty of parents believe sugar makes kids hyper, but the {{empirical}} evidence for that is surprisingly weak.
drill.hint: based on real observations and tests (not *scientific*, *clinical*, *actual* or *hard*)

entries.related: *experimental* — from controlled experiments specifically; *anecdotal* — from personal stories, weaker; *theoretical* — based on ideas, not observation.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Based on an imagined or possible situation rather than a real one.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and discussion: *a hypothetical question*, *a hypothetical situation / scenario*, *purely hypothetical*. People say *This is purely hypothetical, but …* to ask about something sensitive without committing to it. In discussion it also works as a noun for an imagined case (*Let me give you a hypothetical*).
entries.pattern: a hypothetical question / situation / scenario; purely hypothetical
examples: It's a purely **hypothetical** question, but would you ever move abroad for a job?
Officials refused to answer **hypothetical** questions about what would happen if the dam failed.
Let's take a **hypothetical** case: a customer orders online, and the package never arrives.

drill.sentence: Don't panic, I'm not quitting; it was just a {{hypothetical}} question about what I'd do with more free time.
drill.hint: about an imagined situation, not a real plan (not *random*, *general* or *theoretical*)

entries.related: *theoretical* — based on theory rather than practice; *imaginary* — not real at all; *speculative* — based on guesses.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Available only in small amounts, so there is not enough for everyone who needs or wants it.
entries.usage: Common for resources such as water, food, jobs, housing and money: *Jobs are scarce*, *become / grow scarce*, *scarce resources*. It is about supply compared with need, while *rare* means unusual by nature. The adverb *scarcely* has a different meaning, *hardly* (*I could scarcely believe it*).
entries.pattern: be / become / grow scarce; scarce resources / supplies
examples: Affordable apartments are so **scarce** in this city that people line up just to see one.
During the drought, water became so **scarce** that farmers sold half their cattle.
Good mechanics are **scarce** around here, so I drive an hour to the one I trust.

drill.sentence: Fresh vegetables were {{scarce}} on the island in winter, so most families relied on canned food.
drill.hint: available only in small amounts (not *rare* or *limited*)

entries.related: *rare* — unusual by nature, not about need; *in short supply* — the same idea as a fixed phrase; *plentiful* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A standard or point of reference that other things are measured or compared against.
entries.usage: Common in business, finance, education and tech: *set / serve as / become a benchmark*, *a benchmark for* + noun, *the benchmark against which …*. It is also a verb (*We benchmark our prices against competitors*). In everyday speech, *standard* or *yardstick* is often used instead.
entries.pattern: a benchmark for + noun; set / serve as a benchmark; (verb) benchmark A against B
examples: Her first novel became the **benchmark** against which all her later books were judged.
We use the city's median rent as a **benchmark** when deciding if an apartment is a good deal.
The new chip beats its rivals on every standard **benchmark**, but its battery life is still disappointing.

drill.sentence: The crab cakes at that little harbor restaurant are the {{benchmark}} I use to judge every other seafood place in town.
drill.hint: the reference point used for comparison (not *standard* or *yardstick*)

entries.related: *standard* — more general; *yardstick* — similar, slightly informal; *baseline* — the starting point you measure change from.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A mistake, weakness or fault in something or someone that makes it less effective or less than perfect.
entries.usage: Used for plans, arguments, designs, products and characters: *a fatal flaw*, *a design flaw*, *a flaw in the plan / argument*. Note the preposition *in*. For people, *flaws* are character weaknesses (*We all have our flaws*); the adjectives *flawed* (*a flawed system*) and *flawless* (perfect) are very common.
entries.pattern: a flaw in + noun; a fatal / major / design flaw; flawed / flawless
examples: The big **flaw** in his argument is that he's comparing a small town with a city of millions.
The carmaker recalled 200,000 vehicles because of a **flaw** in the braking system.
He's generous and funny, but his biggest **flaw** is that he never admits he's wrong.

drill.sentence: In the show, the detective's fatal {{flaw}} is that she trusts everyone far too easily.
drill.hint: a character weakness, like that of a tragic hero (not *weakness* or *mistake*)

entries.related: *defect* — a fault in a product, more technical; *shortcoming* — a weakness, more formal; *flawless* — perfect, the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Not needed because something else already does the same job or says the same thing.
entries.usage: Common for words, steps, equipment and systems: *a redundant step*, *That sentence is redundant*. In engineering, *redundant* systems are deliberate backups, so there it is a positive word. In British English, *be made redundant* means to lose your job; Americans say *be laid off*.
entries.pattern: a redundant step / word / question; redundant systems (backups); render something redundant
examples: Saying “free gift” is **redundant**; a gift is free by definition.
Once the café started taking card payments at the table, the old register by the door became **redundant**.
Airplanes have **redundant** hydraulic systems, so a single failure won't bring them down.

drill.sentence: Your summary already lists the prices, so repeating them in the last paragraph is {{redundant}}.
drill.hint: not needed because it says the same thing again (not *unnecessary* or *repetitive*)

mistake.wrong: After the factory closed, 300 workers were made redundant.
mistake.right: After the factory closed, 300 workers were laid off.
mistake.why: *Made redundant* in the job sense is British; Americans say *laid off*.

entries.related: *superfluous* — more formal, beyond what is needed; *unnecessary* — plainer; *essential* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Believing that people act mainly out of self-interest, so you doubt that anyone is honest or has good motives.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and journalism: *cynical about* + noun (*cynical about dating apps*), and *a cynical move / ploy* for an action done only for selfish gain. *I'm cynical about it* describes your distrust; *a cynical move* criticizes someone else. German *zynisch* often means mocking in a cruel way; for that, English usually says *sarcastic*.
entries.pattern: cynical about + noun; a cynical ploy / move / attempt; grow cynical
examples: After three bad breakups, she's become pretty **cynical** about dating apps.
The “limited edition” label was a **cynical** marketing ploy to make people pay twice as much.
Fans have grown **cynical** about the team's promises to rebuild after five losing seasons.

drill.sentence: He's so {{cynical}} that when a stranger returned his lost wallet, he assumed she wanted a reward.
drill.hint: convinced people only act for selfish reasons (not *suspicious* or *paranoid*)

mistake.wrong: Stop making cynical comments about my haircut.
mistake.right: Stop making sarcastic comments about my haircut.
mistake.why: Mocking remarks are *sarcastic*; *cynical* means distrusting people's motives, which is narrower than German *zynisch*.

entries.related: *skeptical* — doubting a claim, more neutral; *jaded* — tired and cynical from experience; *idealistic* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + preposition
entries.meaning: To follow a rule, plan, standard or belief closely and consistently.
entries.usage: Formal, typical in official documents, policies, contracts and news: *adhere to the rules / guidelines / a schedule / a diet*, often with *strictly*. In conversation, *stick to* or *follow* is more natural. The noun is *adherence* (*adherence to safety standards*), and an *adherent* is a follower of a belief.
entries.pattern: (strictly) adhere to + rules / guidelines / standards / a schedule / a budget
examples: All restaurants must **adhere to** strict hygiene standards, or they can lose their license.
If you don't **adhere to** the dosing schedule, the antibiotics may not work properly.
The festival **adhered to** its no-plastic policy, so every drink came in a reusable cup.

drill.sentence: Builders who fail to {{adhere to}} the city's building codes can be fined thousands of dollars.
drill.hint: follow closely — formal (not *follow*, *meet*, *comply with* or *abide by*)

entries.related: *comply with* — obey an official rule or order; *stick to* — informal; *deviate from* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Easy to use or understand without instructions or training; also based on feeling rather than conscious reasoning.
entries.usage: The first sense is everywhere in product and tech talk: *an intuitive interface / design / app*, *intuitive to use*. The second describes people and judgments: *an intuitive decision*, *an intuitive sense of*. *Counterintuitive* (surprising, against what you would expect) is also very common.
entries.pattern: intuitive to use; an intuitive interface / design / layout; an intuitive sense / understanding of
examples: The new oven has such an **intuitive** control panel that I never had to open the manual.
She has an **intuitive** sense of what her patients need, even when they can't explain it.
The app is **intuitive** enough that my eighty-year-old neighbor figured it out in a day.

drill.sentence: The ticket machines at the new station aren't very {{intuitive}}, so there's always a line of confused tourists.
drill.hint: easy to understand without instructions (not *user-friendly* or *clear*)

entries.related: *user-friendly* — easy to use, only for products; *instinctive* — done without thinking; *counterintuitive* — the opposite of what you'd expect.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Only on the surface and not deep or thorough; for a person, caring only about appearances and unimportant things.
entries.usage: Neutral for injuries and damage (*superficial cuts*, *superficial damage*), but critical for knowledge, analysis, changes and relationships (*a superficial understanding of*). Calling a person *superficial* is a clear insult; *shallow* is the more everyday word for that.
entries.pattern: superficial damage / cuts / wounds; a superficial understanding / knowledge of; superficial changes
examples: Luckily, the car had only **superficial** damage, just a few scratches on the bumper.
The redesign is mostly **superficial**: new colors and a new logo, but the same slow service.
She ended the relationship because he seemed **superficial** and cared only about looks and money.

drill.sentence: I only have a {{superficial}} knowledge of wine, so I usually just pick the second-cheapest bottle.
drill.hint: on the surface only, not deep (not *basic*, *passing*, *limited* or *shallow*)

entries.related: *shallow* — the everyday word for people; *cursory* — done quickly, without attention; *profound* — deep, the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Producing a lot of money or profit.
entries.usage: Common in business news and in talk about careers: *a lucrative contract / deal / career / market / business*, often with *highly*. It describes deals, jobs and activities, not people: *a lucrative practice*, but *a well-paid lawyer*. It sounds a little more formal than *profitable* or *well-paid*.
entries.pattern: a lucrative contract / deal / career / market / business; highly lucrative
examples: After the Olympics, the swimmer signed a **lucrative** deal with a sportswear brand.
He left teaching for a more **lucrative** career in real estate, but he says he misses the kids.
Selling cold drinks at the beach turned out to be surprisingly **lucrative** for the two teenagers.

drill.sentence: Wedding photography can be very {{lucrative}} if you're willing to work every Saturday all summer.
drill.hint: bringing in a lot of money (not *profitable* or *rewarding*)

entries.related: *profitable* — making a profit, neutral; *well-paid* — for jobs and people; *unprofitable* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Money that a government or organization pays to lower the cost of something or to keep an activity going.
entries.usage: Common in news about the economy and public services: *farm subsidies*, *housing subsidies*, *a subsidy for* + noun, *government subsidies*. Employers can also offer subsidies (*a transit subsidy*, *a gym subsidy*). The verb is *subsidize*, and the adjective *subsidized* is frequent (*subsidized housing*, *subsidized meals*).
entries.pattern: a subsidy for + noun; government / farm / housing / transit subsidies; receive / cut / phase out a subsidy
examples: Thanks to a state **subsidy**, we paid about half the usual price for our new heat pump.
The little museum stays open only because of a yearly **subsidy** from the city.
My employer offers a transit **subsidy**, so my monthly train pass costs me just thirty dollars.

drill.sentence: Without the federal {{subsidy}}, a ticket on that rural airline route would cost over five hundred dollars.
drill.hint: public money that lowers the price (not *funding*, *support* or *grant*)

entries.related: *grant* — a sum given once for a project or study; *tax break* — a lower tax instead of a payment; *subsidize* — the verb.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To win or be accepted in the end, after a struggle or disagreement; also, to be common or widespread in a place or time.
entries.usage: Formal, common in news, law and sports writing: *Common sense prevailed*, *Cooler heads prevailed* (the calm people won), *prevail over / against* an opponent. The second sense appears mostly in the adjective *prevailing*: *the prevailing view*, *prevailing winds*, *the prevailing mood*.
entries.pattern: common sense / justice / cooler heads prevail; prevail over / against + opponent; the prevailing view
examples: The neighbors argued about the fence for months, but in the end common sense **prevailed**.
The underdogs **prevailed** in overtime after trailing for most of the game.
A strange calm **prevailed** in the town as everyone waited for the hurricane to arrive.

drill.sentence: The court case dragged on for three years, but the small bakery finally {{prevailed}} against the giant food company.
drill.hint: came out on top in the end — formal (not *won* or *triumphed*)

entries.related: *win out* — informal; *triumph* — win, with a sense of glory; *predominate* — be the most common, formal.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To repeat an experiment, study or result and get the same outcome; more generally, to copy something exactly.
entries.usage: Central in science: *replicate a study / a finding / results*, *fail to replicate*, and the noun *replication* (*the replication crisis* in psychology). Outside science it means copying a success or a quality: *hard to replicate*, *replicate the success of*. In casual talk, people often say *copy* or *repeat*.
entries.pattern: replicate + a study / finding / result / success; fail to replicate; hard to replicate
examples: Several research teams tried to **replicate** the famous study, but none of them found the same effect.
I've tried for years to **replicate** my mom's chicken soup, but it never tastes quite the same.
The chain hopes to **replicate** the success of its Chicago store in ten more cities.

drill.sentence: No other pizzeria has managed to {{replicate}} that crispy crust; people think the secret is the old stone oven.
drill.hint: make again in exactly the same way (not *copy*, *match*, *recreate*, *reproduce* or *duplicate*)

entries.related: *reproduce* — very close, also used for results; *duplicate* — make an identical copy, often of documents; *imitate* — copy someone's style or behavior.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A system of complicated official rules and procedures that makes things slow and difficult; also the officials who run such a system.
entries.usage: Usually critical in everyday use: *cut through the bureaucracy*, *too much bureaucracy*, *layers of bureaucracy*. It is uncountable for the rules (*so much bureaucracy*) but countable for an organization (*a huge bureaucracy*). *Red tape* is the informal near-synonym, and *a bureaucratic nightmare* is a common complaint.
entries.pattern: cut through / reduce the bureaucracy; layers of bureaucracy; a bureaucratic nightmare
examples: Getting a building permit took nine months because of all the **bureaucracy** at city hall.
She left her hospital job because she spent more time fighting **bureaucracy** than treating patients.
The new office promises to cut through the **bureaucracy** so small businesses can open faster.

drill.sentence: Opening a bank account here involves so much {{bureaucracy}} that I had to visit the branch four times.
drill.hint: slow official procedures (not *paperwork* or *red tape*)

entries.related: *red tape* — informal, the rules themselves; *paperwork* — the forms you fill out; *bureaucrat* — an official, usually said critically.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A rule, law or measure that protects people or things against harm, loss or misuse.
entries.usage: Common in law, finance, health and tech writing, often in the plural: *safeguards against fraud*, *put safeguards in place*, *build in safeguards*. It is also a slightly formal verb (*safeguard your data*, *safeguard children's privacy*). In conversation, *protection* or *safety measure* is plainer.
entries.pattern: a safeguard against + noun; put / build safeguards in place; (verb) safeguard + data / rights / health
examples: The bank added two-step verification as an extra **safeguard** against fraud.
The new rules include **safeguards** to stop teenagers from buying alcohol through delivery apps.
As a **safeguard**, the pool now has a lifeguard at both ends during children's swim lessons.

drill.sentence: Before we hire anyone to redo the roof, let's put some {{safeguards}} in the contract, like paying only after each stage is finished.
drill.hint: protective measures against a bad outcome (not *protections* or *clauses*)

entries.related: *precaution* — a step taken in advance; *protection* — more general; *loophole* — a gap in the rules, almost the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A person you know a little, for example from work or your neighborhood, but who is not a close friend.
entries.usage: Americans use *friend* loosely, so German *ein Bekannter* is often just *a friend* or *someone I know* in English. Calling someone *an acquaintance*, especially *just an acquaintance*, stresses distance and can sound cool. Typical phrases: *a casual / mutual / old acquaintance*; *make someone's acquaintance* is formal and old-fashioned.
entries.pattern: a casual / mutual / old acquaintance; an acquaintance of mine; just an acquaintance
examples: I didn't know anyone at the party except one **acquaintance** from my yoga class.
We met through a mutual **acquaintance** who thought we'd both like hiking.
Reporters described the man as a loner who had a few **acquaintances** but no close friends.

drill.sentence: He's not really a friend, more of a casual {{acquaintance}} I see at the dog park every few weeks.
drill.hint: someone you know only slightly

entries.related: *friend* — closer; *colleague* — someone you work with; *stranger* — someone you don't know at all.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Extremely useful or helpful, so valuable that its worth is hard to measure.
entries.usage: A strong compliment for help, advice, experience and tools: *invaluable advice*, *an invaluable resource*, *invaluable to someone*, *invaluable for* + -ing. Despite the *in-*, it does not mean "without value"; that is *worthless*. It is very common in thank-you notes and recommendation letters (*Your feedback was invaluable*).
entries.pattern: invaluable help / advice / experience / resource; invaluable to someone; invaluable for + -ing
examples: Thanks so much for helping with the move; your truck and your patience were **invaluable**.
The summer I spent in a restaurant kitchen gave me **invaluable** experience in staying calm under pressure.
For new parents, a pediatrician who answers the phone at night is **invaluable**.

drill.sentence: Her years as an ER nurse proved {{invaluable}} when a passenger collapsed on our flight.
drill.hint: extremely useful (not *vital*, *essential*, *crucial* or *priceless*)

mistake.wrong: These old coins are invaluable, so just throw them away.
mistake.right: These old coins are worthless, so just throw them away.
mistake.why: *Invaluable* means extremely valuable; something with no value is *worthless*.

entries.related: *priceless* — so valuable that no price is enough, often for objects or moments; *indispensable* — impossible to manage without; *worthless* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The disadvantage or negative side of something that is otherwise good or attractive.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and business: *the downside of / to* + noun or -ing, *the only downside is …*, *on the downside*. It sounds more relaxed than *disadvantage* or *drawback*. The opposite is *upside* (*The upside is that …*).
entries.pattern: the downside of / to + noun or -ing; the only downside is (that) …; on the downside
examples: The **downside** of living right downtown is that you hear sirens all night.
The job pays well; the only **downside** is the two-hour commute.
Economists warn that the **downside** of very low interest rates is a rise in risky borrowing.

drill.sentence: We love our new puppy, but the one {{downside}} is that nobody in the house has slept past six since.
drill.hint: the bad side of an otherwise good thing (not *drawback*, *problem* or *catch*)

entries.related: *drawback* — same, a bit more formal; *catch* — a hidden problem; *upside* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Thinking only about the near future and not about the long-term effects of a decision.
entries.usage: A common criticism of decisions, policies and plans: *a short-sighted decision / policy*, *It would be short-sighted to …*. Americans often write it as one word, *shortsighted*. For the eye condition, the usual American word is *nearsighted*, while British English says *short-sighted*.
entries.pattern: a short-sighted decision / policy / plan; It's / It would be short-sighted to …
examples: Laying off the whole support team to cut costs was **short-sighted**; within a year, the company had lost half its customers.
It would be **short-sighted** to turn down the internship just because it doesn't pay much.
Many residents called the decision to sell the old park to developers **short-sighted**.

drill.sentence: Skipping retirement savings in your twenties so you can buy a fancier car is pretty {{short-sighted}}.
drill.hint: ignoring the long-term effects (not *reckless* or *irresponsible*)

entries.related: *myopic* — formal, same figurative meaning; *farsighted* — thinking ahead, the opposite; *nearsighted* — the American word for the eye condition.

entries.label: noun (plural)
entries.meaning: Features or services that make a place pleasant or convenient, such as a gym, pool, parking or laundry room.
entries.usage: Typical in apartment listings, hotel websites and travel reviews: *building amenities*, *hotel amenities*, *basic amenities*, *close to local amenities*. It is almost always plural. In hotels it can also mean the small free items in the room, such as soap and shampoo.
entries.pattern: hotel / building / basic / modern amenities; amenities such as …; close to amenities
examples: The rent is high, but the **amenities** include a rooftop pool, a gym and a package room.
The campground has only basic **amenities**: a water pump, two outhouses and some picnic tables.
Young families are moving to the suburb for its good schools, parks and other **amenities**.

drill.sentence: The motel was cheap but had almost no {{amenities}}, not even a coffee maker or a hair dryer.
drill.hint: features that make a stay comfortable (not *facilities*, *extras* or *comforts*)

entries.related: *facilities* — buildings or equipment for a purpose; *perks* — extra benefits, mostly from a job; *conveniences* — things that make life easier.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: In the opposite way; it introduces a statement that reverses the relationship described in the one before.
entries.usage: Formal, mostly in writing, talks and careful explanations; it usually starts a sentence or follows *and* (*and conversely*). It fits best when the second statement mirrors the first (*more A means more B; conversely, less A means less B*), not as a plain *however*. In casual speech, *on the other hand* or *the other way around* is more natural.
entries.pattern: Statement A. Conversely, reversed statement B. / …, and conversely, …
examples: Higher interest rates make saving more attractive; **conversely**, lower rates encourage people to borrow.
Kids who read at home tend to enjoy school more, and **conversely**, kids who enjoy school tend to read more.
A strong defense can hide a weak offense, and **conversely**, a great offense can make up for a shaky defense.

drill.sentence: When the dollar is strong, Americans find Europe cheap to visit; {{conversely}}, a weak dollar makes those trips more expensive.
drill.hint: in the opposite way — formal, one word (not *however* or *in contrast*)

entries.related: *on the other hand* — a general contrast, more casual; *vice versa* — the reverse is also true, at the end of a sentence; *likewise* — in the same way.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To support and keep a law, decision, principle or tradition, especially when it is challenged.
entries.usage: Formal; typical in legal news and official statements. Courts *uphold* a ruling or a conviction, which means they confirm it on appeal (the opposite is *overturn*). Institutions and people *uphold* standards, values, traditions and rights; the past form is *upheld*.
entries.pattern: uphold + a ruling / decision / verdict / ban; uphold standards / values / a tradition
examples: The appeals court **upheld** the ruling that the factory must pay for the river cleanup.
As a teacher, she felt it was her job to **uphold** the school's rules, even the ones she disagreed with.
The family has **upheld** the tradition of a big pancake breakfast on New Year's Day for fifty years.

drill.sentence: After reviewing the video, the league {{upheld}} the player's three-game suspension.
drill.hint: kept in place after a challenge (not *confirmed* or *enforced*)

entries.related: *overturn* — cancel a decision, the opposite; *maintain* — keep at the same level; *defend* — argue for something that is attacked.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To make pain, suffering or a problem less severe, without removing it completely.
entries.usage: Formal; common in medical, news and policy language: *alleviate pain / symptoms / stress / poverty / congestion / concerns*. It suggests partial relief, not a cure. In conversation, *ease* or *relieve* is more natural (*This should ease the pain*).
entries.pattern: alleviate + pain / symptoms / stress / congestion / a shortage / concerns
examples: A warm bath and some gentle stretching helped **alleviate** the pain in my lower back.
The city added more trains at rush hour to **alleviate** overcrowding on the subway.
The manager tried to **alleviate** the staff's fears by promising that nobody would lose their job.

drill.sentence: The new bypass was built to {{alleviate}} the traffic jams that clog the town center every summer.
drill.hint: make less severe — formal (not *ease*, *relieve* or *reduce*)

entries.related: *relieve* — very close, a little less formal; *ease* — everyday; *aggravate* / *exacerbate* — make worse, the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To watch and manage work, a project or a group of people to make sure everything is done correctly.
entries.usage: Common in job descriptions and business news: *oversee a project / construction / operations / a team*. It describes a responsible, higher-level role rather than doing the work yourself; the past forms are *oversaw* and *overseen*. It is a German false friend: *übersehen* (fail to notice) is *overlook* or *miss*.
entries.pattern: oversee + a project / construction / operations / staff; (past) oversaw, overseen
examples: My aunt **oversees** a team of forty nurses at a children's hospital in Denver.
A committee of parents will **oversee** the renovation of the playground.
The festival hired an experienced producer to **oversee** the stage crews and the sound checks.

drill.sentence: As head chef, she {{oversees}} everything that leaves the kitchen, from the bread to the desserts.
drill.hint: is in charge of and checks (not *supervises* or *manages*)

mistake.wrong: Sorry, I oversaw your email yesterday.
mistake.right: Sorry, I overlooked your email yesterday. / Sorry, I missed your email yesterday.
mistake.why: *Oversee* means supervise; for German *übersehen* (fail to notice), say *overlook* or *miss*.

entries.related: *supervise* — watch people closely as they work; *manage* — be in charge of, more broadly; *overlook* — fail to notice, a different word.

entries.label: verb + preposition
entries.meaning: To get something such as pleasure, income or meaning from a particular source; *derive from* or *be derived from* also means to come from that source.
entries.usage: Neutral to formal: *derive pleasure / satisfaction / income / benefit from*, and for words and ideas *be derived from* or *derive from* (*The word derives from Latin*). It sounds more formal than *get from* or *come from*. In math, *derive* a formula means work it out step by step, which is a separate sense.
entries.pattern: derive + pleasure / satisfaction / income / benefit from + noun; X derives from / is derived from Y
examples: My dad **derives** more pleasure from fixing old radios than from anything else.
The word “robot” **derives from** a Czech word for forced labor.
Most of the town's income is **derived from** tourism and fishing.

drill.sentence: Many retirees {{derive}} a real sense of purpose from volunteering at the local food bank.
drill.hint: take from a source — slightly formal (not *get*, *gain*, *find* or *draw*)

entries.related: *stem from* — come from, usually for problems; *originate* — begin in a place or time; *draw on* — use as a source.

entries.label: verb + preposition
entries.meaning: To treat a person or group unfairly or worse than others because of a characteristic such as age, sex, race, religion or disability.
entries.usage: Common in law, news and HR language: *discriminate against* + group, often with *on the basis of* (*on the basis of age*), and in the passive *be discriminated against*. In this sense it always needs *against*. *Discriminate between* (tell apart) is a separate, neutral and more formal use.
entries.pattern: discriminate against + person / group (on the basis of + age / sex / disability …); be discriminated against
examples: The law makes it illegal to **discriminate against** job applicants on the basis of age.
The airline was fined for **discriminating against** passengers who use wheelchairs.
She felt she was **discriminated against** at work after she announced she was pregnant.

drill.sentence: Several restaurants were accused of {{discriminating against}} customers with service dogs by refusing to seat them.
drill.hint: treating unfairly because of who they are

mistake.right: The company discriminated against older applicants.
mistake.why: In the unfair-treatment sense English needs *against*; German *jemanden diskriminieren* has no preposition.

entries.related: *be biased against* — have an unfair attitude toward; *prejudice* — an unfair opinion formed in advance; *discriminate between* — tell apart, a neutral sense.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To find a way for two ideas, facts or needs that seem to conflict to exist together or make sense together.
entries.usage: The typical patterns are *reconcile A with B* and *reconcile A and B* (*reconcile work and family life*), often with *hard / difficult / impossible to reconcile*. *Reconcile yourself to* something means to accept a situation you don't like. The verb also means to make peace between people (*They reconciled after years apart*) and, in accounting, to make two sets of numbers agree.
entries.pattern: reconcile A with B / A and B; hard / impossible to reconcile; reconcile yourself to + noun
examples: It's hard to **reconcile** his kindness to strangers with the way he treats his own brother.
Many parents struggle to **reconcile** a full-time job with picking up the kids at three.
The two witness statements were impossible to **reconcile**: one said the car was red, the other blue.

drill.sentence: I couldn't {{reconcile}} the glowing online reviews with the cold food and rude service we actually got.
drill.hint: make two conflicting things fit together (not *square* or *match*)

entries.related: *square A with B* — informal, make agree; *balance* — give time or weight to both; *contradict* — be inconsistent with, almost the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To cause a strong reaction, especially anger, criticism or protest; also, to annoy someone on purpose so that they react.
entries.usage: Very common with reactions as the object: *provoke outrage / anger / a backlash / debate / a reaction*. With a person as the object it means annoy them deliberately (*Don't provoke him*), often as *provoke someone into* + -ing. The adjective *provocative* (meant to cause a reaction) can be a compliment for art and ideas.
entries.pattern: provoke + outrage / anger / criticism / debate / a reaction; provoke someone (into + -ing)
examples: The decision to cancel the parade **provoked** angry calls to city hall from local shop owners.
My little brother knows exactly what to say to **provoke** me, and he enjoys it.
The dog isn't aggressive; it only bit because the kids **provoked** it by pulling its tail.

drill.sentence: The price increase {{provoked}} so many angry comments that the company reversed it within a week.
drill.hint: led to a strong angry reaction (not *caused*, *drew*, *sparked*, *prompted* or *triggered*)

entries.related: *trigger* / *spark* — start a reaction suddenly; *incite* — encourage violence or crime, stronger; *provocative* — meant to provoke.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Boring and tiring because it takes a long time, is slow, or repeats the same thing again and again.
entries.usage: Used most often for tasks and processes: *a tedious task / process / job*, *tedious paperwork*, *tedious but necessary*. It stresses slowness and repetition more than *boring* does: a movie is usually *boring*, while entering data by hand is *tedious*. It sounds a little more formal than *boring*.
entries.pattern: a tedious task / process / job; tedious to do; tedious but necessary
examples: Peeling three bags of potatoes for the school fundraiser was **tedious**, but chatting with friends made it fun.
Filling out the same medical history form at every new doctor's office is incredibly **tedious**.
The negotiations were long and **tedious**, but both sides eventually signed the deal.

drill.sentence: Removing old wallpaper is a {{tedious}} job: you scrape off one tiny strip at a time for hours.
drill.hint: dull because it is slow and repetitive (not *boring*, *slow* or *messy*)

entries.related: *boring* — general; *monotonous* — always the same, with no variety; *mind-numbing* — informal, extremely tedious.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A public claim that someone has done something wrong or illegal, made before it has been proven.
entries.usage: Common in news, law and business: *make / face / deny / investigate an allegation*, *allegations of fraud / misconduct*, *allegations against* someone. It is careful language: it reports a claim without saying it is true. *Alleged* and *allegedly* are used for the same reason (*the alleged thief*).
entries.pattern: allegations of + noun; allegations against + person; make / face / deny / investigate allegations
examples: The restaurant owner denied **allegations** that he had underpaid his kitchen staff.
The school board is investigating **allegations** of cheating on the state exam.
She made a serious **allegation** against her former business partner, but she had no documents to back it up.

drill.sentence: The company has hired an outside law firm to investigate {{allegations}} of bribery inside its sales team.
drill.hint: unproven public claims of wrongdoing (not *claims*, *charges*, *reports* or *accusations*)

entries.related: *accusation* — similar, can be more personal; *claim* — more general; *charge* — a formal accusation by police or prosecutors.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Probably not true, honest, safe or good, so it should not be trusted; said of a person, feeling unsure or doubtful.
entries.usage: Very common: *a dubious claim / source / practice*, *of dubious quality / value*. With a person, *be dubious about* something means you doubt it. The ironic phrase *the dubious honor / distinction of* (something bad presented as an award) is well known.
entries.pattern: a dubious claim / source / practice; of dubious quality / value; be dubious about + noun
examples: The website sells “miracle” supplements with some very **dubious** health claims.
Our town has the **dubious** honor of having the worst potholes in the state.
I was **dubious** about the cheap hotel, but it turned out to be clean and quiet.

drill.sentence: He bought the “designer” watch from a guy on the street, so its origins are {{dubious}} at best.
drill.hint: probably not legitimate (not *questionable*, *shady*, *suspect* or *doubtful*)

entries.related: *questionable* — very close; *suspicious* — causing the feeling that something is wrong; *doubtful* — unlikely, or uncertain.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To form ideas or guesses about causes, reasons or future events without having enough information to be sure.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation, often as a refusal: *It's too early to speculate*, *I don't want to speculate*. Patterns: *speculate about / on* + noun, *speculate that* + clause. In finance it also means buying property or shares in the hope of a quick profit; the noun is *speculation* (*pure speculation*).
entries.pattern: speculate about / on + noun; speculate that …; It's too early to speculate
examples: Police wouldn't **speculate** about the cause of the fire until the investigation was finished.
Fans have been **speculating** for months about who will play the lead in the new movie.
We can only **speculate** on why the previous owners painted every room purple.

drill.sentence: The doctor said it was too early to {{speculate}} about how long my recovery would take.
drill.hint: make guesses without enough facts (not *guess*, *predict* or *say*)

entries.related: *guess* — informal; *hypothesize* — form a theory to test, academic; *conjecture* — formal, guess from incomplete evidence.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To make someone decide not to do something, usually by making them afraid of the consequences or by making it harder.
entries.usage: Common in law, safety and security contexts: *deter crime / thieves / burglars*, *deter someone from* + -ing. The passive *not be deterred by* is frequent (*Don't be deterred by the price*). The noun *deterrent* (*a strong deterrent*) is just as common; note the double *r* in *deterred*, *deterring*.
entries.pattern: deter + crime / thieves; deter someone from + -ing; not be deterred by + noun
examples: Bright lights and a loud dog are often enough to **deter** burglars.
The high fines are meant to **deter** people from texting while they drive.
The rain didn't **deter** thousands of fans from lining up outside the stadium all night.

drill.sentence: We put a fake owl on the roof to {{deter}} pigeons from nesting near the gutters.
drill.hint: put off by making them afraid (not *stop*, *prevent*, *keep* or *discourage*)

entries.related: *discourage* — milder, can be through words; *prevent* — make it impossible; *deterrent* — something that deters.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To gradually collect or increase in amount over a period of time.
entries.usage: Used with an object (*accumulate wealth / debt / experience / evidence*) and without one (*Dust accumulates under the bed*). It is frequent for things that build up slowly or unnoticed: dust, snow, debt, clutter, interest. In conversation, people often say *build up* or *pile up*.
entries.pattern: accumulate + wealth / debt / experience / evidence; dust / snow / interest accumulates
examples: Snow **accumulated** so quickly overnight that we couldn't open the front door in the morning.
Over thirty years, my parents **accumulated** an amazing amount of stuff in the garage.
If you only pay the minimum, interest **accumulates** and your credit card debt keeps growing.

drill.sentence: Use the vacuum attachment to clean behind the fridge, where dust and pet hair {{accumulate}}.
drill.hint: increase little by little — slightly formal, one word (not *collect* or *gather*)

entries.related: *build up* / *pile up* — everyday; *amass* — formal, collect a lot, often money; *accumulation* — the noun.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Belonging to the basic nature of something or someone, rather than coming from outside.
entries.usage: Formal; common in psychology, economics, philosophy and serious discussion: *intrinsic value*, *intrinsic motivation* (doing something because you enjoy it), *intrinsic to* + noun. The opposite is *extrinsic* (from outside, such as rewards or pay). In casual speech, *built-in* or *basic* is plainer.
entries.pattern: intrinsic value / motivation / quality; intrinsic to + noun; an intrinsic part of
examples: Kids who read for **intrinsic** reasons, not for prizes, usually keep reading as adults.
A dollar bill has almost no **intrinsic** value; it's worth something only because people trust it.
Some risk is **intrinsic** to starting a business; you can reduce it, but you can't avoid it.

drill.sentence: Psychologists call the urge to do something because you enjoy it, not for money or praise, {{intrinsic}} motivation.
drill.hint: coming from inside a person or thing (the standard term; the opposite is *extrinsic*)

entries.related: *inherent* — very close, often for risks and problems; *integral* — necessary to make something complete; *extrinsic* — coming from outside, the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Making people think seriously about a subject, often in a new way.
entries.usage: A typical compliment in reviews and conversation: *a thought-provoking book / film / talk / question / article*. Its tone is positive but calm, so it fits both casual and formal settings. It is written with a hyphen both before a noun and after a verb (*The film was thought-provoking*).
entries.pattern: a thought-provoking book / film / talk / question / discussion
examples: The documentary about food waste was really **thought-provoking**; I've changed how I shop.
Our book club had a **thought-provoking** discussion about whether the main character was a hero.
The museum's new exhibit asks some **thought-provoking** questions about what a city chooses to remember.

drill.sentence: Her talk on loneliness among young adults was so {{thought-provoking}} that the audience kept asking questions for an hour.
drill.hint: making people reflect seriously (not *interesting*, *inspiring* or *engaging*)

entries.related: *stimulating* — interesting and full of ideas; *insightful* — showing deep understanding; *provocative* — meant to cause a strong, often angry reaction.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very interested and curious to know more about something, often because it is unusual or mysterious.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing: *I'm intrigued*, *intrigued by* + noun, *intrigued to hear / learn / see*. It is stronger and more personal than *interested* and suggests a small mystery. The adjective *intriguing* describes the thing that causes the feeling (*an intriguing idea*).
entries.pattern: be intrigued by + noun; intrigued to hear / learn / see; I'm intrigued
examples: I was **intrigued** by the tiny bookstore with no sign, so I went in.
“I have news, but I can't tell you until Friday.” “Okay, now I'm **intrigued**.”
Investors were **intrigued** by the startup's plan to rent out garden tools to neighbors.

drill.sentence: The cooking class promised “Italian food without pasta,” and I was {{intrigued}} enough to sign up.
drill.hint: drawn in by something unusual (not *curious* or *interested*)

entries.related: *curious* — wanting to know, more general; *fascinated* — extremely interested; *intriguing* — describes what makes you intrigued.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Something that is different from what is normal or expected, so it does not fit the usual pattern.
entries.usage: Common in science, statistics, finance and news: *a statistical anomaly*, *an anomaly in the data*, *detect anomalies*. In everyday speech it often means a one-time exception (*That loss was an anomaly*). The adjective *anomalous* is formal and mostly academic.
entries.pattern: an anomaly in + noun; a statistical anomaly; just / merely an anomaly
examples: The team's loss to the last-place team was an **anomaly**; they've won every other game this season.
The bank flagged the charge as an **anomaly** because I had never bought anything in Brazil before.
One patient's unusually fast recovery turned out to be an **anomaly**, not a sign that the treatment worked.

drill.sentence: Our electric bill doubled in March, but that was an {{anomaly}}: a broken heater had been running all month.
drill.hint: something unusual that breaks the normal pattern (not *exception*, *outlier* or *aberration*)

entries.related: *outlier* — a data point far from the rest; *exception* — a case that does not follow a rule; *fluke* — informal, a lucky or unlucky accident.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To become or make something smaller, weaker or less important.
entries.usage: Used without an object (*The pain gradually diminished*) and with one (*diminish the risk*). With people and achievements it means making them seem less important, often unfairly (*I don't want to diminish what she did*). The fixed phrase *diminishing returns* means each extra effort brings less benefit.
entries.pattern: diminish + the risk / value / importance / role; not diminish someone's achievement; diminishing returns
examples: The swelling **diminished** after a few days, but I still couldn't run.
I don't want to **diminish** what you did, but the whole team helped close that deal.
As the factories closed, the town's role as a regional center slowly **diminished**.

drill.sentence: Losing the final doesn't {{diminish}} what the team achieved this season; they still beat every top seed.
drill.hint: make seem less important (not *change*, *erase* or *lessen*)

entries.related: *decrease* / *reduce* — plainer, often for numbers; *dwindle* — become gradually fewer; *belittle* — make someone seem unimportant, more personal.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Short and clear, using only the words needed and leaving out unnecessary detail.
entries.usage: A positive word for writing and speaking: *a concise summary / answer / email / report*, *clear and concise*. *Concise* is always praise, while *short* only gives the length and *terse* can sound rude. The noun is *conciseness* or *concision*.
entries.pattern: a concise summary / answer / explanation / email; clear and concise
examples: Her email was polite and **concise**: three sentences, a link and a deadline.
The instructions in the box are refreshingly **concise**, with pictures instead of long paragraphs.
Applicants should write a **concise** cover letter that explains why they want the job.

drill.sentence: Keep your wedding toast {{concise}}; nobody wants a twenty-minute speech before dinner.
drill.hint: to the point, with no extra words (not *short* or *brief*)

entries.related: *brief* — short in time or length; *succinct* — very close, slightly more formal; *wordy* / *long-winded* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Completely new and very important, introducing ideas or methods that change how things are done.
entries.usage: Common in news, reviews and marketing: *groundbreaking research / work / discovery / technology / film*. It is strong praise, so in advertising it can sound like hype. American English usually writes it as one word; a *groundbreaking ceremony* is the literal event that starts construction of a building.
entries.pattern: groundbreaking research / discovery / work / film / technology
examples: Her **groundbreaking** research on sleep changed how hospitals schedule night shifts.
When it came out in 1999, the movie's special effects were truly **groundbreaking**.
The company calls its new vacuum **groundbreaking**, but it looks just like last year's model.

drill.sentence: The surgeon became famous for a {{groundbreaking}} heart operation that no one had ever tried before.
drill.hint: completely new and highly important (not *revolutionary*, *pioneering* or *innovative*)

entries.related: *pioneering* — being the first to do something; *revolutionary* — causing huge change; *cutting-edge* — the most advanced right now.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Suggested or understood without being stated directly.
entries.usage: Common in serious discussion, law and academic writing: *an implicit assumption / message / threat / agreement*, *implicit in* + noun. The opposite is *explicit*. A separate fixed use is *implicit trust* or *trust someone implicitly*, which means complete trust without any doubt.
entries.pattern: an implicit assumption / message / threat / agreement; implicit in + noun; trust someone implicitly
examples: We had an **implicit** agreement in our apartment that whoever cooked didn't have to wash the dishes.
**Implicit** in her question was the idea that we hadn't tried hard enough.
Many of the software's errors come from an **implicit** assumption that every user speaks English.

drill.sentence: Nobody said it out loud, but the message was {{implicit}}: if sales didn't improve, the store would close.
drill.hint: understood without being stated (not *clear*, *obvious* or *unspoken*)

entries.related: *explicit* — stated clearly, the opposite; *implied* — suggested by what someone says; *tacit* — formal, understood without words (*tacit approval*).
